item.title: How to Blur WhatsApp Messages During a Screen Share
item.description: Learn how to blur WhatsApp messages, chats, names, and media before sharing your screen in a meeting, demo, support call, or recording.
item.content:encoded:
Screen sharing makes small WhatsApp details suddenly important. A message preview can appear in the sidebar, a contact name can identify a private conversation, and a profile photo can tell people more than you intended.
The safest fix is not to rely on noticing every message before it appears. Prepare WhatsApp Web before you start sharing, choose the right browser surface, and keep sensitive parts of the page blurred while the call is running.
**Privacy Blur for WhatsApp is a free Chrome extension that blurs chats, messages, names, and media on WhatsApp Web during screen sharing.** It runs on the WhatsApp Web page and gives you separate controls for the parts of the interface you want to hide.
![WhatsApp Web before applying message blur, with the Privacy Blur control panel visible](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-before.png)
## Why WhatsApp messages can appear during screen sharing
When you share a browser tab or window, viewers can see the content rendered inside that surface. WhatsApp Web may show more than the message you were reading:
- The active conversation and message text - Chat names in the left sidebar - Last-message previews - Contact names and profile photos - Images, videos, and other media - Text in the compose box - Status or About information
Chrome’s own screen-sharing guidance recommends sharing a tab instead of your entire screen when possible. Sharing the whole screen can expose unrelated notifications, open applications, bookmarks, and other personal information. That browser-level choice is useful, but it does not blur private content inside the WhatsApp tab. The WhatsApp page still needs its own visual privacy layer.
The steps below focus on WhatsApp Web in Chrome. They are useful for team meetings, client demos, support calls, tutorials, recordings, and any situation where someone else may see your browser.
## Step 1: Open WhatsApp Web before the call
Open [web.whatsapp.com](https://web.whatsapp.com/) and wait for your chats to finish loading. Do this before the meeting starts, not while someone is waiting for you to share.
If you use Privacy Blur for WhatsApp, its floating widget appears on the WhatsApp Web page. Open the widget and review the available blur controls. The extension only runs on WhatsApp Web; it does not change other tabs or your desktop.
This is also a good time to close unrelated tabs and applications. A WhatsApp blur extension can hide content inside WhatsApp Web, but it cannot protect a banking tab, a private document, or a notification that appears somewhere else on your screen.
## Step 2: Turn on message blur
In the Privacy Blur panel, enable the control for messages. This applies a visual blur to message text in the active conversation so people watching the shared surface cannot casually read it.
Do not stop at the open conversation. Send a test message to yourself or open a safe chat and check how the page looks. WhatsApp Web updates dynamically, so confirm that newly rendered message rows receive the blur as well.
The goal is not to make WhatsApp unusable. It is to make the sensitive text unreadable at a glance while leaving enough of the interface visible for you to navigate.
![WhatsApp messages and media blurred while the Privacy Blur controls remain available](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-messages-blurred.png)
![Privacy Blur for WhatsApp panel with separate controls for messages, names, previews, and media](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/privacy-blur-panel.png)
## Step 3: Hide chat names and previews
Message text is only one part of the privacy problem. The sidebar can expose a conversation even when the open message area is covered.
If the call is sensitive, enable the controls for:
- Chat-list names - Contact names - Message previews - Profile photos
Choose the smallest set that matches your situation. A product demo may need the interface to remain readable, while a personal call or public recording may justify a broader blur.
This selective approach is useful because different screen-sharing situations have different risks. You might hide names and previews during a client call but leave the general WhatsApp layout visible. For a recording that will be published, you may prefer to blur more of the page.
Read the visible header before you begin sharing. If it identifies a person, group, company, or private topic, blur the contact or conversation name as well as the message body.
## Step 4: Use the global toggle before sharing
If you do not want to inspect each zone separately, use the global toggle. It gives you a fast way to turn the privacy layer on before you select a screen or browser surface.
A practical routine looks like this:
1. Open the Privacy Blur widget. 2. Select the message and surrounding-context zones you need. 3. Turn on the global blur state. 4. Inspect the active chat, sidebar, header, media, and compose area. 5. Start sharing only after the visible page looks safe.
The global toggle is especially useful when a meeting begins unexpectedly. You can enable the broad privacy state first, then adjust individual zones when there is time.
![WhatsApp Web fully blurred with the Privacy Blur panel available for adjusting individual zones](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-full-blurred.png)
## Step 5: Check media and the compose box
A conversation can reveal private information without showing a readable message. A photo, video thumbnail, document preview, or draft reply can be enough.
Before sharing, check whether you also need to blur:
- Images and videos inside the conversation - Profile photos and avatars - The message compose box - Status or About information - Link previews and other message attachments
The compose box deserves a separate check. If you type while sharing, viewers may see the draft before you send it. Blur it when you are demonstrating WhatsApp or switching between conversations during a call.
If your use case is a tutorial, use a test account or a conversation with dummy content. Blur is a safety layer, not a reason to put real private messages on display for a recording.
## Step 6: Choose the safest Chrome sharing option
Chrome’s [screen-sharing guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/avoiding-oversharing-when-screen-sharing/) explains why sharing a tab usually exposes less unrelated information than sharing the entire screen. Use that principle when your meeting tool offers the choice.
Prefer, in order:
1. The specific WhatsApp Web tab, when the meeting tool supports tab sharing 2. A browser window containing only the intended work 3. The entire screen only when you genuinely need it
Sharing a tab does not replace message blur. Someone watching that tab can still read whatever WhatsApp displays. It simply reduces the chance of exposing unrelated apps, notifications, bookmarks, or other browser tabs.
Before clicking Share, read the selected surface out loud or in your head. It is easy to choose the wrong tab when several browser windows are open.
## Step 7: Test the page from a viewer’s perspective
Do one final pass before the meeting:
- Can you read the active message? - Can you identify the contact from the header? - Can you read names or previews in the sidebar? - Are profile photos visible? - Is a media thumbnail recognizable? - Is anything sensitive visible in the compose box? - Did you select the intended Chrome tab or window?
If possible, join the call from another device or ask a teammate to confirm what they can see. A local view can look safe while a scaled-down shared view still makes names or previews readable.
Privacy Blur supports hover reveal for cases where you need to inspect one blurred area locally. Use it carefully: reveal only what you need, then move the pointer away and confirm that the rest of the page remains blurred.
## Keep the blur enabled while the call is running
WhatsApp Web changes as new messages arrive and as you move between conversations. Do not assume that a page checked at 9:00 AM will remain safe for a 9:30 AM demo.
Keep the global blur state enabled while sharing. If you need to open a different conversation, check the header and sidebar again after the page updates. If someone sends a new message, let the blur remain active before you read it.
For recurring workflows, Privacy Blur Pro adds persistence, keyboard shortcuts, keyword rules, and sender rules. Keyword rules can help when certain phrases should always be hidden, while sender rules can help keep specific conversations blurred. These controls are still visual privacy features; they do not encrypt WhatsApp or protect content from browser developer tools.
## What WhatsApp message blur does not protect
It is important to keep the promise narrow. A browser blur extension helps hide visible content from people watching the shared page. It does not:
- Encrypt WhatsApp messages - Protect the underlying page from browser developer tools - Hide content in another tab, app, or device - Prevent someone with account access from reading WhatsApp elsewhere - Replace careful selection of the shared tab or window - Guarantee that a recording contains no private information
Read the product’s [privacy policy](https://amrita-labs.com/privacy-blur-whatsapp/privacy/) if you want to understand what runs locally and what product analytics are separate from WhatsApp content. Message text, contact names, and media are not sent to Amrita Labs for the blur operation.
## A simple pre-share checklist
Save this short routine for your next meeting:
1. Open WhatsApp Web early. 2. Open Privacy Blur and enable message blur. 3. Hide names, previews, profile photos, and media if needed. 4. Turn on the global toggle. 5. Check the active chat, sidebar, header, and compose box. 6. Share the specific WhatsApp tab or window instead of the whole screen when possible. 7. Test the viewer’s perspective. 8. Keep the blur enabled while new messages and conversations load. 9. Stop sharing before changing privacy settings or opening another private page.
The routine takes less time after you have used it a few times. More importantly, it moves privacy preparation before the moment when other people are already watching.
## Try Privacy Blur for WhatsApp
If you need to blur WhatsApp messages during screen sharing, [try Privacy Blur for WhatsApp](https://amrita-labs.com/privacy-blur-whatsapp/?utm_source=amrita-labs&utm_medium=owned-content&utm_campaign=whatsapp_blur_messages&utm_content=blog_cta). It gives you message, name, preview, media, profile-photo, and compose controls directly on WhatsApp Web, with a global toggle for fast preparation.

item.description: Compare Chrome extensions that blur WhatsApp Web chats, names, previews, and media during screen sharing, meetings, demos, and recordings.
item.content:encoded:
Screen sharing turns an ordinary WhatsApp Web tab into a privacy risk. A chat preview can expose a private message, a contact name can reveal who you are talking to, and a profile photo can identify someone before you notice what is visible in the shared window.
Privacy Blur for WhatsApp is a free Chrome extension that blurs chats, messages, names, and media on WhatsApp Web during screen sharing. It is designed for the practical problem: keep WhatsApp open, but decide which parts of the interface other people can see.
This guide compares Chrome extensions that add a visual privacy layer to WhatsApp Web. The useful differences are not just whether an extension can blur a message. Look at what it can hide, whether you can reveal one item without exposing everything, whether it includes a screen lock, and whether its privacy model is clear.
![WhatsApp Web fully blurred with Privacy Blur controls visible during a screen-sharing preparation workflow](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-full-blurred.png)
## What a WhatsApp privacy extension should protect
WhatsApp Web exposes more than the open conversation. Depending on the page state, people nearby or viewers of a shared window may see:
- The active contact or group name - Chat names in the left sidebar - Last-message previews - Profile photos and avatars - Message text and timestamps - Photos, videos, and other media - Text in the compose box - Status or About information
A useful extension lets you choose the level of protection. You may want to blur everything before a client call, or hide only message previews while working in a shared office. Hover reveal is also important: it lets you read one item locally without removing the blur from the rest of the page.
![WhatsApp Web before applying privacy blur, with the Privacy Blur control panel visible](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-before.png)
## Quick comparison
| Extension | Best for | Notable controls | |---|---|---| | [Privacy Blur for WhatsApp](https://amrita-labs.com/privacy-blur-whatsapp/?utm_source=amrita-labs&utm_medium=owned-content&utm_campaign=whatsapp_blur_launch_2026-11&utm_content=best-extensions) | Selective zone control during sharing, demos, and recordings | Independent blur zones, hover reveal, global toggle, optional keyword and sender rules | | [Blur for WhatsApp Web](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/blur-for-whatsapp-web-blu/dfclcielfgmlbnoilehbkgblednpnkkn) | Broad blur plus a screen lock | Blurs names, profile pictures, messages, and other sensitive content; optional PIN lock | | [WhatsApp Web Privacy Blur](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/whatsapp-web-privacy-blur/dkckbpalmbhdlcdacgcgabjgilkmpjil) | A simple WhatsApp-focused privacy layer | Blur chats, names, photos, previews, and media; hover reveal and password lock | | [WhatsApp Privacy - Blur & Lock](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/whatsapp-privacy-blur-loc/nilmencjidekakalbadokifapilcgboi) | Users who want blur controls plus a local lock | Blurs messages, previews, names, photos, media, and the compose area; includes screen-lock features |
Chrome Web Store listings and features can change. Check the current listing, permissions, update date, and privacy disclosure before installing any extension that operates on WhatsApp Web.
## 1. Privacy Blur for WhatsApp — best for choosing exactly what stays private
[Privacy Blur for WhatsApp](https://amrita-labs.com/privacy-blur-whatsapp/?utm_source=amrita-labs&utm_medium=owned-content&utm_campaign=whatsapp_blur_launch_2026-11&utm_content=best-extensions) is built around independent controls instead of one all-or-nothing blur. Its panel lets you choose messages, contact names, chat-list names, preview text, profile photos, the compose box, images and videos, and Status or About information.
That matters when your screen-sharing situation changes. Before a team meeting, you may enable every zone. During a support call, you may keep the chat visible but hide names and previews. When recording a tutorial, you may blur messages and media while leaving the interface readable.
The global toggle provides a fast way to switch the whole privacy layer on or off. Hover reveal lets you inspect a blurred item locally while the rest of the page stays protected. New WhatsApp content can continue to appear while the blur controller watches the changing page.

The product page explains that WhatsApp chat content, contact names, and media are not sent to Amrita Labs; blur logic runs locally in the browser. Anonymous product analytics and billing events are separate from message content.
Choose this option if your main problem is not only “blur WhatsApp,” but “blur the right parts of WhatsApp for this particular call.”
![Privacy Blur for WhatsApp panel showing independent blur-zone controls and hover reveal](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/privacy-blur-panel.png)
## 2. Blur for WhatsApp Web — best for broad blur plus a PIN lock
[Blur for WhatsApp Web](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/blur-for-whatsapp-web-blu/dfclcielfgmlbnoilehbkgblednpnkkn) focuses on hiding names, profile pictures, messages, and other sensitive content. Its Chrome Web Store description also highlights an optional PIN lock for the WhatsApp screen.
That combination fits users who want a straightforward privacy mode and a stronger barrier when they step away from the computer. It is less about building a detailed workflow around separate zones and more about quickly hiding the information most likely to be exposed in a shared room or meeting.
Check whether its current controls match the parts of WhatsApp you need to hide. If you need separate switches for chat-list previews, media, the compose box, and status information, compare those controls directly in the current listing and extension UI.
## 3. WhatsApp Web Privacy Blur — best for a focused WhatsApp-only blur layer
[WhatsApp Web Privacy Blur](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/whatsapp-web-privacy-blur/dkckbpalmbhdlcdacgcgabjgilkmpjil) is another focused option for hiding chats, names, photos, previews, and media. Its listing describes hover reveal, a password lock, local browser controls, and no account requirement.
This type of extension works well for someone who wants a small privacy layer without changing how WhatsApp works. The important check is whether the extension still receives updates as WhatsApp Web changes. Read the listing’s update information and recent reviews, then test the exact screens you use before relying on it for a live presentation.
As with any browser extension that runs over private conversations, treat the privacy disclosure as part of the feature set. “Blur” describes what viewers see; it does not automatically tell you what the extension can access or transmit.
## 4. WhatsApp Privacy - Blur & Lock — best for a lock-oriented workflow
[WhatsApp Privacy - Blur & Lock](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/whatsapp-privacy-blur-loc/nilmencjidekakalbadokifapilcgboi) combines visual blur with a local screen-lock concept. Its listing describes controls for messages, previews, names, profile pictures, media, and the message input area, along with a password lock for the page.
This is useful if your concern continues after the meeting ends. Blur reduces accidental exposure while the tab is visible; a lock can help when you leave the workstation. Those are different jobs, so confirm whether the lock behavior, inactivity handling, and recovery flow fit your setup.
Avoid treating a browser lock as encryption. It is a visual and access-control layer inside the browser. It does not protect WhatsApp data from browser developer tools, malware, or someone who can access the underlying account.
![WhatsApp Web messages and media blurred while the Privacy Blur panel remains available for local controls](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-messages-blurred.png)
## How to choose between them
Start with the exact privacy problem:
### You need selective controls
Choose an extension with separate zones if you want to hide chat names but keep the interface readable, or hide message previews without covering the entire page. Selective controls reduce the temptation to turn privacy protection off because the whole page became unusable.
### You need a quick all-page mode
A broad blur toggle is useful immediately before a meeting or recording. Test it on the active chat, sidebar, profile photo, and media viewer. A control that covers only the open message area may leave identifying information elsewhere on the page.
### You need to inspect one message privately
Look for hover reveal and test it with the cursor. The desired behavior is local: you reveal one area on your screen while other viewers continue to see the rest blurred. Do not assume every extension uses the same reveal behavior.
### You leave WhatsApp open in shared spaces
A screen lock can complement blur. Use it when you step away from a laptop, work in a coworking space, or switch from a private task to a public presentation. Confirm whether the lock is local, how it is triggered, and what happens after reload.
### You care about message privacy
Read the extension’s privacy disclosure before installing. Prefer clear explanations of permissions, local processing, analytics, billing, and data retention. A privacy tool should not require vague trust when it operates over private conversations.
## A safe screen-sharing routine
Before sharing your screen:
1. Open WhatsApp Web and wait for the page to finish loading. 2. Enable the zones you need to hide. 3. Check the active chat, chat list, header, profile photo, media, and compose box. 4. Turn on the global blur mode if you do not want to inspect each zone separately. 5. Start sharing only the intended browser tab or window. 6. If you need to read one message, use hover reveal rather than disabling all blur. 7. Turn the privacy layer back on before switching chats. 8. Stop sharing before changing privacy settings or opening unrelated private pages.
The extension reduces accidental exposure, but it does not replace careful screen-sharing habits. Do not claim that a blur extension encrypts WhatsApp, hides content from browser developer tools, or protects a different tab, desktop app, or device.
## Final recommendation
For a simple blur-and-lock workflow, compare the lock-focused extensions first. For a configurable screen-sharing workflow, Privacy Blur for WhatsApp is the strongest fit when you want independent zones, hover reveal, and a fast global toggle on WhatsApp Web.
The right choice is the one you can verify on the exact WhatsApp screens you share. Test the sidebar, active conversation, previews, media, profile photos, and compose box before your next meeting. A privacy extension earns its place when it makes that check quick and repeatable.

item.title: How to Write Better Pinterest Pin Titles and Descriptions
item.description: Write Pinterest Pin titles and descriptions that make the topic clear, add useful context, and stay aligned with the image, board, and destination.
item.content:encoded:
A Pinterest Pin title has one job before it has any chance to be clever: make the topic clear.
The description should then answer the next question. What will someone find after they click or save this Pin? Who is it for? What makes this version useful?
**Pinello is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags — in real time.** It gives creators a pre-publish review while the draft is still easy to change.
You don’t need a giant keyword list to write better Pin copy. You need a clear subject, a specific audience or use case, and enough detail to make the destination believable.
![Pinello Pin Doctor showing title and description checks inside the Pinterest Create Pin workflow](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/title-description-expanded.png)
## Start with the phrase a real person would search
Before writing, finish this sentence:
> This Pin is about ______ for ______.
For an Etsy seller, that might be “handmade ceramic mugs for cozy kitchen gifts.” For a blogger, it could be “easy vegetarian meal prep recipes for busy weekdays.” For a print-on-demand creator, it might be “funny teacher appreciation shirts for elementary teachers.”
That phrase gives you a useful starting point for the title. It is more helpful than beginning with a brand slogan or a vague line such as “You need this” or “New ideas.”
Keep the audience and subject close together. “Bedroom decor” is broad. “Small bedroom storage ideas for renters” gives the reader a clearer reason to stop.
The phrase does not need to be the final title. Think of it as a plain-language brief. Once you know what the Pin actually promises, you can make the wording sound more like your brand.
## Put the main topic early in the title
Pinterest’s [creative best practices](https://business.pinterest.com/en-gb/creative-best-practices/) list a title limit of 100 characters and note that the first 40 characters are most likely to show. That is a useful reason to lead with the subject, not a reason to cram a title with keywords.
Compare:
- **Weak:** “A Few Things I Loved This Week” - **Stronger:** “Small Bedroom Storage Ideas for Renters”
The stronger version is not trying to sound like an advertisement. It says what the Pin contains. You can add one useful qualifier after the main topic:
- “Easy Meal Prep Recipes for Busy Workweeks” - “Minimalist Wedding Invitation Ideas for 2026” - “Funny Book Lover T-Shirts for Readers” - “How to Style a Small Entryway Without Renovating”
Specificity does not mean adding every related phrase to one title. Choose the primary topic, then add one detail that changes who the Pin is for, what format it uses, or what problem it solves.
### Remove warm-up words
Words such as “look,” “amazing,” “must-see,” and “you’ll love this” use space without explaining the Pin. They can work in a sentence after the subject, but they should not hide the subject.
Instead of:
> “You’ll love these amazing ideas for your home”
Try:
> “Renter-Friendly Entryway Ideas for Small Homes”
The second title gives the reader something concrete to understand. It also gives you a better test: does the destination actually contain renter-friendly entryway ideas?
## Make the description complete the title
Do not repeat the title and stop. Use the description to add the information a reader still needs.
If the title is **Small Bedroom Storage Ideas for Renters**, the description could say:
> “Make a small rental bedroom feel less crowded with removable shelves, under-bed storage, and simple layout ideas. These practical solutions work without permanent changes.”
That description adds the audience, the approach, and a reason to click. It sounds like normal language instead of a list of search phrases.
For an Etsy product Pin:
> “A handmade stoneware mug with a soft speckled glaze, made for slow mornings and thoughtful kitchen gifts. See the full size and color details before ordering.”
For a blog Pin:
> “These vegetarian meal prep recipes use simple ingredients and hold up well for weekday lunches. Save the list when you need practical dinners without a long grocery trip.”
The description has a job. It can explain the product, set expectations for the article, name a constraint, or make the next step obvious. It does not need to repeat the title word for word.
Pinterest’s [product-feed guidance](https://business.pinterest.com/en-ca/blog/optimize-your-product-feed-tips/) makes the same broader point: titles and descriptions should contain meaningful, specific information. It gives product examples such as brand, colour, features, and other details that help explain what is being shown. For a normal content Pin, translate that principle into the details that matter for your audience.
Read the first sentence on its own. If it starts with “Check this out” or “I’m so excited,” replace the warm-up with the actual topic.
## Use related terms where they belong
Natural variations can make a description clearer:
- “small bedroom storage” and “renter-friendly organization” - “vegetarian meal prep” and “make-ahead lunches” - “teacher appreciation shirt” and “gift for elementary teachers”
Use the words because they help explain the Pin, not because you are trying to hit an invisible quota. Pinterest’s guidance supports using meaningful broad and specific phrases, but that does not mean turning the description into a keyword pile.
For example:
> “Small bedroom storage, bedroom organization, storage ideas, small space storage, renter storage, bedroom ideas, home organization.”
That list may contain relevant terms, but it does not help someone understand what they will find. A sentence does:
> “Use removable shelves, under-bed bins, and narrow storage pieces to organize a small bedroom without making permanent changes.”
The second version includes useful language naturally. It also gives the reader a reason to believe the article or product will help.
## Keep title, description, image, and board aligned
Copy cannot fix a Pin package that tells four different stories.
Imagine the image shows a printable weekly meal planner, the title says “Healthy Dinner Recipes,” the description talks about grocery budgeting, and the selected board is “Home Office Ideas.” Each individual field might sound reasonable. Together, they create doubt.
Read these four pieces together:
1. Image 2. Title 3. Description and topics 4. Selected board
Ask whether a person could explain the Pin’s subject in one sentence. If not, decide which field contains the real promise, then bring the others closer to it.
This is especially important for creators who publish across several audiences. An Etsy product may be a necklace, a personalized gift, and a Mother’s Day item. The best title and board depend on which reason the Pin is leading with. Don’t make every possible angle equally loud.
## Check the four avoidable copy problems
Before publishing, look for these common issues:
### 1. The first words are filler
Move the subject forward. “New ideas for…” is usually weaker than naming the actual topic.
### 2. The title is too broad
Add an audience, use case, format, room, season, or constraint. “Meal ideas” becomes “Easy Freezer Meals for Busy Families.”
### 3. The description only repeats the title
Add practical detail, a differentiator, or an accurate next step. The reader should learn something new.
### 4. The fields disagree
If the title says “small apartment storage” but the image and destination are about luxury home renovations, revise the package before publishing.
Pinello’s Pin Doctor turns these checks into a pre-publish review. It checks the image, title, description, topics, board match, and SEO fields, then highlights one focus issue instead of handing you a wall of vague advice.
When a rewrite would help, you can request a copy-only suggestion such as **Strengthen title** or **Improve description**. The result goes to your clipboard. Pinello does not type into Pinterest fields or publish the Pin for you, so you can edit the wording until it sounds like your brand.
![Pinello Pin Doctor showing a copy-only title or description suggestion before it is copied to the clipboard](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/pin-doctor-copied-ai.png)
## Use a simple title formula, then make it sound human
Templates help when you are staring at a blank Create Pin form:
**Title:** `[primary topic] for [audience or use case]`
**Description:** `[what the Pin offers]. [specific detail, benefit, or constraint]. [natural next step if appropriate].`
Examples:
**Title:** “Printable Wedding Budget Checklist for First-Time Couples”
**Description:** “Keep venue, vendor, and ceremony costs in one simple wedding budget checklist. Use the printable version to plan deposits and spot missing categories before they become surprises.”
**Title:** “Small Balcony Garden Ideas for Renters”
**Description:** “Make a rental balcony more useful with compact containers, easy-care plants, and layouts that don’t require permanent changes. Use these ideas when you want more greenery in a small space.”
It is not a magic formula. It is a way to make the first draft concrete enough to improve. Once the copy is clear, remove anything that sounds generic or unlike you.
## Rescore after you edit
Do not treat a Pin score as a verdict on your creativity. Use it as a checklist signal.
For example, a draft may start with:
**Title:** “Cute Desk Ideas”
After deciding what the Pin actually offers, you might revise it to:
**Title:** “Small Desk Setup Ideas for a Calm Home Office”
Then make the description explain the setup, audience, and constraints. If the relevant checks improve, the revised Pin is easier to review before you publish. That still does not tell you how many saves, clicks, or impressions it will get. It tells you that the draft is more complete against the checks you can inspect.
![Pinterest Pin Doctor before a copy repair, showing a vague title, short description, and unfinished fields](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-before.png)
![Pinterest Pin Doctor after a copy repair, showing clearer title and description text with a ready-to-review status](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-after.png)
That boundary is useful. You can improve what is in front of you without claiming to know the future.
## A quick final review
Before you publish, read the title and description without looking at the image. Can you tell what the Pin is about and who it is for?
Then look at the image and board. Do they support the same promise?
Finally, check the destination. If the Pin sends people to a product page, article, or shop listing, the wording should prepare them for what they will see after the click.
If one field is weak, fix that field first. You don’t need to rewrite everything just because one sentence is vague.
For a repeatable second set of eyes, [see how Pinello checks Pinterest Pins before publishing](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=amrita-labs&utm_medium=owned-content&utm_campaign=pinello_titles_descriptions&utm_content=blog_cta). It keeps the review beside the Create Pin workflow, with copy-only suggestions when you choose to ask for them.

That’s not helpful when you’re preparing a batch of Etsy product Pins, writing a blog Pin between client calls, or trying to turn a POD design into a clear product post. You don’t need another dashboard full of warnings. You need to know which weakness is worth fixing first.
Pinello’s Pin Doctor is built for that moment. [Pinello](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=amrita-labs&utm_medium=owned-content&utm_campaign=pinello_launch_2026-11&utm_content=pin-doctor-fix-weakest-part) is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags — in real time. Inside Create Pin, Pin Doctor shows the SEO Audit and uses **Focus next** to point to the most important unfinished part.
![Pinello Pin Doctor reviewing an Etsy-style Pinterest draft with Focus next and a ready-to-review status](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/etsy-pin-doctor.png)
## What the Pin Doctor checks
Doctor looks at the pieces you can still change:
- The image and its available quality details - The Pin title - The description - Topics and hashtags - The selected board and board fit - SEO-related fields available in the draft
Some checks are deterministic, such as whether a required field is blank or whether an image detail is available. Other guidance is Pinello’s own heuristic review. The interface uses source labels to make that difference visible:
- **From Pinterest** - **Pinello check** - **AI suggestion** - **Not provided by Pinterest**
That’s a useful guardrail. A suggestion can help you rewrite a sentence, but it isn’t an official Pinterest instruction.
## Start with Focus next, not with every warning
Open the Doctor and look for the top issue. If the title is vague and the description is empty, don’t spend ten minutes choosing hashtags first. Fix the issue that makes the Pin hardest to understand.
Focus next can turn a broad review into one manageable action:
1. Read the issue. 2. Open the related field or repair action. 3. Edit the draft in Pinterest, or use a copy-only suggestion. 4. Return to the Doctor. 5. Check the before-and-after rescore.
You’re not trying to make the score perfect in one click. You’re making the next decision clearer.
![Pinello Pin Doctor showing a focused next action for a draft that still needs topics](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/focus-on.png)
## Example: an Etsy product Pin
Imagine a seller has a Pin for a handmade linen apron.
The image is attractive, but the title says “Kitchen Things.” The description says “Available now in my shop.” The topics include “home decor” and “summer style.” The selected board is “Recipe Inspiration,” which contains food photography but very few product Pins.
The weakest part isn’t the image. It’s the package around the image.
Focus next might lead the seller to:
- Change the title to “Handmade Linen Apron for Home Cooks” - Explain the fabric, use, or gift context in the description - Replace unrelated topics with terms that match the apron - Check whether a kitchen textiles or handmade gifts board is a better fit
If the board choice remains uncertain, the seller can trigger Board Match explicitly after selecting the candidate board. That result is a Pinello recommendation, not a prediction of distribution.
After the edit, the before-and-after rescore shows whether the draft improved against Pinello’s checks. The seller still decides whether the copy sounds like the brand.
## Example: a blog Pin with a strong image but weak copy
Bloggers often start with a good hero image and then rush the fields. Consider a Pin with a clear photo of a small balcony garden. The title is “Garden Ideas,” and the description is blank.
The repair doesn’t require a new design. It needs clarity:
- Title: “Small Balcony Garden Ideas for Beginners” - Description: “Plan a small balcony garden with container-friendly herbs, flowers, and layout ideas for renters and apartment dwellers.” - Topics: balcony gardening, container gardening, beginner garden ideas - Board: a focused gardening board rather than a general inspiration board
The result is more useful because every field supports the same topic. That’s the kind of improvement a pre-publish review can verify.
![Pinterest Pin Doctor before a repair, showing a weak title, short description, and missing topics](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-before.png)
![Pinterest Pin Doctor after a repair, showing clearer copy and a ready-to-review status](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-after.png)
## When to use a copy-only AI suggestion
Pinello includes user-triggered actions such as **Strengthen title**, **Improve description**, and **Refine topics**. Use them when you know the field needs help but you’re stuck on wording.
The output is copy-only. Pinello places the suggestion on your clipboard for you to review and paste. It doesn’t type into Pinterest fields, change your Pin automatically, or publish it.
Treat the suggestion as a draft. Check:
- Does it describe the actual product or article? - Does it preserve your voice? - Does it make a claim you can support? - Does it match the image and destination? - Would a customer understand it quickly?
If the answer is no, edit it or ignore it. A shorter human sentence is often better than a polished sentence that says the wrong thing.
## Read the SEO Audit without chasing a magic grade
SEO Audit is part of Pin Doctor, not a separate promise that Pinello knows Pinterest’s ranking system. Use it as an organized review of visible fields.
For each item, ask what kind of evidence you’re seeing:
- A missing title is a concrete completeness issue. - An image ratio or resolution check is a technical image review. - A topic mismatch is a relevance judgment based on the draft. - A Board Match result is Pinello’s recommendation. - A rewrite is an AI suggestion you can accept, change, or reject.
This keeps the tool in the right role: diagnosis and repair before publishing.
## The before-and-after rescore is the useful loop
The first score is a snapshot of the draft as it was. The second score tells you whether the changes improved Pinello’s checks.
That loop is helpful for small edits:
- Add the missing description and rescore - Replace the vague title and rescore - Choose a closer board and rescore - Remove an unrelated topic and rescore
You can learn what changed without pretending the number represents future saves, clicks, reach, ranking, or virality. It measures the draft against the checks Pinello can run.
## Don’t fix the weakest part by making everything louder
A common reaction to a weak Pin is to add more text, more hashtags, and more design elements. That can make the Pin harder to read.
Fix the actual weakness. If the image is cluttered, simplify it. If the title is vague, make it specific. If the board is wrong, choose a better fit. If the description is empty, add context. More fields are not automatically better fields.
## A repair order that works for batch creation
When you’re reviewing ten Pins at once, use the same order every time:
**image → title → description → topics → board**
Start with the image because the copy can’t rescue a Pin that doesn’t communicate its subject. Then make the title specific enough to stand on its own. Add a description that explains the product, article, or idea. Check that topics and hashtags describe that same subject. Finish by checking the selected board and running Board Match if the choice is close.
This order also helps when several fields are weak at once. A clearer title often makes the right topics easier to choose. A more specific title can reveal that the board is too broad. One repair can expose the next useful repair without turning the workflow into a full rewrite.
For a POD creator, that might mean replacing a generic “New Shirt” title before deciding whether the Pin belongs on a niche gift board. For a blogger, it might mean clarifying that a “garden ideas” post is specifically for renters before choosing between a gardening board and a small-space board.
You can still publish a Pin with an imperfect preference call. The point is to resolve the obvious weaknesses first, then make a deliberate final review.

item.title: Pinterest Pin Scorer: Feed Score vs Pin Detail Score vs Pin Doctor
item.description: Understand how Pinello's Feed Score, Pin Detail Score, and Pin Doctor fit together when you inspect and improve Pinterest Pins.
item.content:encoded:
A Pinterest Pin can look different depending on where you inspect it. In the feed, you see a compact card. In the closeup, you can review more of the Pin's details. In Create Pin, you are working on a draft that you can still change.
**[Pinello](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=amrita-labs&utm_medium=owned-content&utm_campaign=pinello_launch_2026-10&utm_content=feed-detail-score-pin-doctor) is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags — in real time.** It places three related surfaces around those three moments: Feed Score while you browse, Pin Detail Score when you open a Pin, and Pin Doctor while you prepare your own Pin.
These surfaces belong to one workflow, but they are not interchangeable. Each one answers a different question: Which Pins are worth a closer look? What can I learn from this Pin's fuller context? What should I fix in my own draft before publishing? ![Pinello Feed Score badges displayed on Pinterest feed cards](/assets/blog/pinello/feed/feed-score.png)
## The short version
| Pinello surface | Where you see it | What it is for | |---|---|---| | **Feed Score** | Pinterest feed cards | A quick signal while you browse | | **Pin Detail Score** | The Pin closeup | A fuller inspection using the information available there | | **Pin Doctor** | Pinterest Create Pin | Pre-publish checks and guidance on the next fix |
The numbers can differ because the surfaces have different inputs. That is not a bug, and it is not a promise that one number is the "real Pinterest score." These are Pinello's own quality-review signals based on the information available at that moment.
## 1. Feed Score: a quick signal while you browse
Feed Score is designed for speed. As you browse Pinterest, Pinello adds score badges to feed cards so you can decide which Pins deserve a closer look.
This is useful when you are:
- Collecting inspiration for a new Etsy listing - Reviewing Pins in a niche before designing your own - Looking for examples of title and description patterns - Comparing several Pins without opening every one - Saving promising Pins to local Favorites for later
The feed card does not always expose every field available inside the Pin closeup. A Feed Score is therefore a browse-time signal, not a complete inspection.
The surrounding context still matters. Depending on what Pinterest exposes, Pinello can show creator and board context, visible stats, and other details that help you understand what you are looking at. Those details are useful for research, but they should not be treated as an official Pinterest measurement or as an explanation of future distribution.
### When to use Feed Score
Use Feed Score when you are moving quickly through a feed and want a compact way to prioritize what to inspect next. You do not need to stop and analyze every Pin. Start with the Pins that are relevant to your topic, then open the ones that contain useful examples or context.
For example, an Etsy seller planning a nursery-art collection might browse several related searches, note which Pins are visually clear, and save a few useful references. Feed Score helps keep that first pass lightweight.
Do not copy another creator's wording or assume that a score explains why a Pin received attention. Use the feed view to collect examples and questions for your own publishing workflow.
## 2. Pin Detail Score: inspect the closeup
Pin Detail Score appears when you open a Pin. The closeup can expose fuller information than the feed card, such as the title, description, board, image dimensions, creator context, visible stats, and other available Pin metadata.
With that fuller view, Pinello can recompute its score using more inputs. A Pin that received a partial Feed Score may receive a different Pin Detail Score simply because more information is now available.
![Pinello Pin Detail Score and Pin context shown in the Pinterest closeup](/assets/blog/pinello/pin-details/feed-score-comparison-with-pin-detail-1.png)
Use the closeup to ask better questions:
- What does the title actually say? - Does the description add useful context? - Which board is attached? - Are the image dimensions and presentation what you expected? - What creator and board context is visible? - Which details are supplied by Pinterest, and which are Pinello checks?
You can also save the Pin to local Favorites. Favorites keep useful research in your browser, where you can filter or sort saved Pins by available score and review them later. This creates a reference set without turning a score into a claim about what will happen next.
### Why Feed Score and Pin Detail Score may not match
Imagine a feed card with a strong image and a short visible title. Feed Score may use that limited information. When you open the Pin, the closeup may reveal a blank description, a different board context, or additional metadata. Pin Detail Score can account for the fuller view.
The reverse can happen too. A field may be unavailable, incomplete, or exposed inconsistently. Pinello shows the score it can calculate from the current evidence and uses source labels where the distinction matters.
The practical interpretation is simple:
- **Feed Score** is a quick browse-time check. - **Pin Detail Score** is a fuller closeup check.
Neither one is an official Pinterest ranking score, and neither one predicts reach, saves, clicks, or future performance.
## 3. Pin Doctor: improve your own draft
Pin Doctor is the creation-side surface. It appears inside Pinterest's Create Pin workflow, where you can still edit the image, title, description, topics, and board.
Instead of helping you choose what to inspect, Pin Doctor helps you decide what to fix next. Depending on the available fields and the current draft, it includes:
- Image checks - Title checks - Description checks - Topic and hashtag checks - Board-related checks - SEO Audit - A publish-status chip - Focus next for the most important issue - Before-and-after rescore after you revise the draft
![Pinello Pin Doctor showing SEO Audit and the pre-publish review workflow](/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/pin-doctor.png)
The distinction is important. Feed Score and Pin Detail Score help you inspect Pins you are browsing. Pin Doctor is for the Pin you are preparing to publish.
### When to use Pin Doctor
Open Pin Doctor after you have chosen the Pin's direction and are ready to review the draft. Start with SEO Audit and Focus next rather than trying to change everything at once.
If the title is vague, rewrite it so the topic is clearer. If the description is empty, add useful context in natural language. If the selected board does not fit the Pin, review the board choice and run the explicit Board Match check when appropriate.
When you use an AI action, Pinello returns a copy-only suggestion to your clipboard. You choose whether to paste it, edit it, or ignore it. Pinello does not publish the suggestion for you, and the final wording remains your decision.
After making a change, review the draft again. The before-and-after rescore helps you see whether the change improved the checks that were available for that draft.
## A practical browse-to-publish workflow
### Step 1: Browse with Feed Score
Start on Pinterest and look for Pins relevant to the topic, audience, and format you are researching. Use Feed Score to prioritize which examples deserve more attention. Save useful references to Favorites rather than opening every card immediately.
### Step 2: Inspect promising Pins with Pin Detail Score
Open a small set of Pins and compare their closeup details. Look at titles, descriptions, boards, image treatment, and visible creator or board context.
You are building a better brief for your own Pin: what is clear, what is missing, and which decisions seem intentional. Pinello can help you inspect those fields. It does not tell you that another Pin will win or that your version will receive a particular result.
![Pinello comparison view showing the transition from a feed signal to fuller Pin detail](/assets/blog/pinello/pin-details/feed-score-comparison-with-pin-detail-2.png)
### Step 3: Improve your own draft with Pin Doctor
Create your Pin, select the board, and open Pin Doctor. Start with the highest-priority issue, make a focused revision, and review the result again.
This order keeps research and creation separate. You can learn from the context around existing Pins without copying them, then apply the useful lessons to a draft that belongs to you.
## Source labels keep the scores understandable
Pinello uses plain labels to distinguish what you are seeing:
- **From Pinterest** — information exposed by Pinterest - **Pinello check** — a local or rule-based review - **AI suggestion** — copy generated only after you request an action - **Not provided by Pinterest** — information the platform does not expose to Pinello
This distinction is especially useful when reviewing Board Match or a copy suggestion. Those are Pinello tools for decision support, not official Pinterest judgments.
## Which surface should you use?
Use **Feed Score** when you are moving quickly through a feed and want a compact signal.
Use **Pin Detail Score** when a Pin is worth opening and you want fuller context.
Use **Pin Doctor** when the Pin belongs to you and you can still edit it before publishing.
You do not need to choose one surface forever. A creator can browse for inspiration, inspect a saved example, and then switch to Pin Doctor for the actual publishing workflow.
## What none of these scores means
None of these surfaces predicts reach, virality, ranking, saves, clicks, timing, or future performance. Pinterest's own systems and user behavior include information outside the fields a browser extension can inspect.
Pinello's narrower promise is more practical: it makes visible checks easier before you publish. You can improve a vague title because it is vague. You can choose a board because it fits the Pin. You can repair an incomplete description because it leaves out the point. Those are decisions you can make before publishing without pretending to know the future.
## Try the full inspect-to-improve workflow
[See the Pinello workflow for browsing, inspecting, and improving Pins](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=amrita-labs&utm_medium=owned-content&utm_campaign=pinello_launch_2026-10&utm_content=feed-detail-score-pin-doctor). The landing page shows where Feed Score, Pin Detail Score, and Pin Doctor fit without asking you to treat any one number as a guarantee.

item.title: Azure Functions ESM Imports: The Silent Bug That Deploys Fine and Registers 0 Endpoints
item.description: If your Azure Functions v4 deploy succeeds but no endpoints show up, a missing .js extension in an ESM import can crash cold start without obvious deploy errors.
item.content:encoded:
I had one of those deploys that makes you question your own eyesight. `func azure functionapp publish` said everything was fine. Azure Portal showed a healthy Function App. My local tests passed. The build passed. Then I ran `az functionapp function list` and got... nothing.
Not broken endpoints. Not one broken endpoint. Zero endpoints registered.
I lost about four hours to this before the fix turned out to be one boring, insulting detail: I was missing `.js` on a relative import.
## The setup looked healthy
This was the stack:
- Azure Functions v4 - Node.js 22 - TypeScript - `"type": "module"` in `package.json` - Clean local runs
Which is exactly why this bug is so annoying. Everything around the app looks healthy. Azure uploads the code just fine. The runtime is what falls over.
## The actual ESM import problem in Azure Functions
In Node ESM, relative imports need file extensions. Every time. TypeScript does not magically exempt you from that.
```typescript // ❌ Looks fine in dev, fails in production Node ESM import { logLlmCall } from "../telemetry";
// ✅ What the runtime actually needs import { logLlmCall } from "../telemetry.js"; ```
That mismatch was the whole issue.
TypeScript compiled happily. Vitest ran happily. My editor did not complain. But once Azure tried to load the compiled JavaScript, Node followed ESM rules strictly, hit `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, and the Functions host never finished registering the app.
## Why Azure Functions feels silent when this breaks
This is the part that made the whole thing feel cursed.
The deploy command can still succeed because the package upload is fine. The Function App can still start. The failure happens during cold start, when the runtime walks your module graph. If one import is wrong, the app crashes before Azure registers any functions.
So from the outside, it looks like a successful deployment with a mysteriously empty Function App. The real error usually lives in Application Insights, not in the publish output.
## How I finally diagnosed it
The first useful command was this:
```bash az functionapp function list --name your-func-app --resource-group your-rg ```
If that returns an empty array right after a "successful" deploy, I would assume cold-start failure until proven otherwise.
From there, Application Insights told the truth. In **Traces**, filtering for `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` made the problem obvious.
## The fix was annoyingly simple
I went through every relative import in my TypeScript source and added `.js`:
```typescript import { coherenceScore } from "./scoring.js"; import { logLlmCall } from "../telemetry.js"; import { CACHE_TTL } from "../../shared/constants.js"; ```
Yes, importing `.js` from a `.ts` file feels wrong the first time you do it.
Yes, it is still the right thing to do for Node ESM.
After that, the exact same deployment registered endpoints normally.
## What I would check before every Azure Functions ESM deploy now
If I were doing this from scratch again, I would add a quick pre-deploy check for imports missing `.js` in the built output:
```bash grep -rn "from \"\.\." dist/ | grep -v "\.js\"" | grep -v "node_modules" ```
If that returns anything, I would stop there and fix it before touching Azure.
## Two other Azure Functions + ESM gotchas I hit
While I was in this rabbit hole, two more sharp edges showed up:
1. **`func azure functionapp publish` needs `FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME`** either in `local.settings.json` or via the `--javascript` flag. Without it, you get "Can't determine project language." 2. **The npm-installed `func` CLI can break on newer Node versions**. On Node 26+, I had better luck with `winget install Microsoft.Azure.FunctionsCoreTools`.
If you are deploying a Chrome extension backend or any small Node service to Azure Functions, this is worth checking early. When ESM imports are wrong, Azure does not always scream. Sometimes it just smiles, deploys, and gives you an app with no functions.
---

item.title: I Built a Chrome Extension That Scores Your Gmail Subject Lines — Here's What I Learned
item.description: After watching my cold emails die in spam folders, I built a tool that scores subject lines in real time. Here's what actually makes email subjects work.
item.content:encoded:
A few months ago I was sending cold emails for a side project. Personalized openers, clear asks, short paragraphs — I thought the emails were good. But my reply rate was garbage. Like, 1-2% garbage.
I started digging into why. Turns out most of my emails weren't even being opened. They were landing in spam or getting ignored at the subject line.
The frustrating part? I'd spend 20 minutes writing a thoughtful email body, then slap on a subject line in 5 seconds. "Quick question." "Following up." "Hey!" Basically handing Gmail's spam filter a reason to bury me.
So I did what any engineer would do when annoyed enough — I built something.
## What I actually built
[EmailSubjectScore Pro](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dleffnbdjohkmmkbojehdpkgkmpofmgm) is a Chrome extension that sits inside Gmail's compose window. As you type a subject line, it scores it on three things:
- **Spam risk** — are you triggering filters without realizing it? - **Clarity** — does the recipient know what this email is about? - **Urgency** — is there a reason to open it now vs. never?
If your subject scores poorly, you hit "Suggest rewrite" and the AI proposes alternatives. You pick one, it drops into the subject field. Done.
No external tabs. No copy-pasting. It just... sits there in Gmail and tells you when your subject line sucks.
![EmailSubjectScore Pro scoring a subject line inside Gmail compose — green score means ready to send](/assets/blog/emailsubjectscore-cws.png)
## The three things I learned about subject lines
Building the scoring engine forced me to study what actually works. Most subject line advice online is recycled fluff. But three patterns kept showing up in the data:
**Spam triggers are sneakier than you think.** Everyone knows to avoid "FREE" and "ACT NOW." But "just checking in" and "quick question" are also flagged now — they've been so overused by sales automation that Gmail treats them as spam signals. The extension catches these in real time, which is something I didn't expect to be so useful for myself.
**Specific beats clever, every time.** "Thought you'd find this interesting" tells the recipient nothing. "Your onboarding flow has a 60% drop-off at step 3" tells them exactly why they should care. The best subject lines make a promise so specific that the person can decide in 2 seconds whether it's worth opening. No mystery, no games.
**Front-load or die.** On a phone lock screen, you see maybe 30-35 characters of a subject line. If your important words come after "Hey [Name], I just wanted to reach out because..." — nobody will ever see them. The extension penalizes subjects where the keywords are buried past character 40. Sounds obvious, but I was doing it constantly before I had a score staring me in the face.
## Before and after
Some real examples from my own emails:
| Before | After | |---|---| | "Quick question" | "Can you review these 3 vendor proposals by Friday?" | | "Following up" | "The pricing expires June 30 — here's the breakdown" | | "Hey!" | "Your AWS bill is 3x higher than similar companies" |
The befores aren't terrible emails written by terrible people. They're what happens when you're in a rush and don't think about it. The afters are what happens when something nudges you for 5 seconds.
![EmailSubjectScore Pro showing rewrite suggestions for a weak subject line](/assets/blog/best-email-subject-line-extensions-hero.png)
## Where it's at
100 + installs within a month so far, organic CWS traffic. It's early but also tells me that it is a common problem.
The free tier gives you 50 AI scores per month and 10 per day. Enough to cover a normal person's important emails without hitting a wall.
If you try it and something feels off — a score that doesn't make sense, a rewrite that sounds weird, a bug where it doesn't show up in compose — genuinely tell us. We're building this for people who send emails that matter, and the best feedback comes from people actually using it.
**→ [Install EmailSubjectScore Pro (free)](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dleffnbdjohkmmkbojehdpkgkmpofmgm)**

item.title: How to Tell If Your Pinterest Pin Will Perform (Before You Post)
item.description: Before a pin gets traction, it usually passes a few predictable checks. These are the signals we look at before publishing when we want stronger Pinterest performance.
item.content:encoded:
Some Pinterest pins feel dead on arrival.
You post them, maybe give them a day, and it is obvious they are not going anywhere. Then another pin — sometimes one you spent less time on — keeps getting impressions, saves, and clicks for weeks. That used to feel random to me. The more pins I watched, the less random it looked.
A lot of the difference shows up before the pin is even published. Pinterest gets an immediate set of signals from the image, the board, the title, the description, and then the first wave of engagement. If those signals are weak, the pin rarely gets much room to recover.
[Pinello](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/kmelegdnljikegoemigfgnpcbllmkije) is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and keywords — in real time, directly on pinterest.com.
![Pinterest pin scoring checklist — 5 dimensions to check before posting](/assets/blog/pinterest-chrome-extensions-pinello.png)
This is the pre-publish check I use when I want a pin to have a better shot.
## The first 24 hours matter more than people think
Pinterest is not purely chronological, but early signals still matter.
If a pin gets a decent first impression — people stop, save, or click — Pinterest has a reason to keep showing it. If the pin looks confusing, mismatched, or under-optimized, it often stalls before it gets that chance.
That is why I care so much about the stuff that is fixable *before* I post.
## The 5 signals I look at before posting a pin
### 1. Will the image stop the scroll?
Before I think about keywords, I do the thumbnail test.
Pinterest is visual, and the image gets judged fast. I usually stick to **2:3 vertical format (1000×1500px)** because it fills the feed cleanly without weird cropping. Then I ask a few blunt questions:
- Is the pin readable on a phone? - Is there one clear focal point? - Does the text overlay help, or is it fighting the image? - Does the topic make sense in a second or less?
If the thumbnail looks muddy or crowded, the rest of the pin has to work too hard.
### 2. Does the board make the topic obvious?
The board is not just a folder. It is context.
A pin about weeknight recipes belongs on a board that sounds like weeknight recipes, not a vague catch-all board with a cute name. The stronger the board context, the easier it is for Pinterest to understand what audience the pin belongs with.
I want the board to do three things:
- use a searchable topic phrase - already contain enough related pins to feel coherent - make the new pin feel obviously on-theme
When I save a great pin to a lazy board, I usually regret it later.
### 3. Does the title carry the keyword early enough?
A good Pinterest title does not need to be fancy. It needs to be legible, specific, and front-loaded.
Only part of the title gets real attention in the feed, especially on mobile, so I try to get the key phrase near the front. Titles like these do a clearer job:
- "Minimalist Bedroom Ideas for Small Spaces" - "25 Modern Bathroom Ideas Under $500" - "2026 Wedding Color Trends"
What I avoid are titles that waste the opening on filler: "Check this out," "I love this," "Great tips," and so on. They may sound friendly, but they do not help Pinterest or the reader understand the pin.
### 4. Does the description give Pinterest enough context?
This is where a lot of pins quietly underperform.
If the description is blank, Pinterest has less text to work with. If the description is robotic, it feels stuffed. I want something in the middle: enough context to reinforce the topic, but still readable.
Usually that means **100-300 characters** and 2-3 natural sentences.
I also do not waste space on hashtag stuffing here. On Pinterest, that space is better spent on plain-language keywords that actually describe the pin.
For example:
> "Easy 30-minute chicken stir fry recipe with vegetables. A simple weeknight dinner idea for busy families who still want something healthy. Save this for your next meal prep day."
That does not try too hard. It just tells Pinterest, and the reader, what the pin is for.
### 5. Am I giving the pin a decent first-day chance?
This is the signal people skip because it feels less tangible.
The first 24 hours still matter. Saves are strong. Clicks help. Even just stopping the scroll matters more than a pin getting tossed into the void at a random time.
So before I post, I try to think about distribution too:
- Am I posting when my audience is actually around? - Is this going to the most relevant board first? - Do I have a reason to expect early saves or clicks?
I do not obsess over timing hacks, but I do not pretend timing is irrelevant either.
## My pre-publish Pinterest pin checklist
Before every pin, I run through this:
| Dimension | ✅ Ready to post | ❌ Fix first | |---|---|---| | Image | 2:3 ratio, bright, readable at thumbnail | Square/landscape, dark, tiny text | | Board | Keyword title, 10+ pins, topically matched | Creative name, empty, random mix | | Title | Keyword in first 40 chars, specific | Vague, starts with filler words | | Description | 100-300 chars, 2-3 keywords, CTA | Empty, one sentence, hashtag spam | | Timing | Peak hours for your audience | Random time, no thought to scheduling |
If even one row feels weak, I usually fix it. That is much easier than trying to diagnose a flop afterward.
## What I automate now
You can absolutely do this checklist manually. I still do, sometimes.
But if you are publishing a lot of pins, the easy mistakes pile up. Wrong board. Weak title. Empty description. Image resized badly in a rush. That is why we built Pinello to score those dimensions directly on pinterest.com while the pin is still in front of you.
The main benefit is not that it predicts the future perfectly. It is that it catches the obvious misses before they become performance problems.
## The few changes that fix most weak pins
If I had to simplify all of this down to the handful of fixes that matter most, it would be these:
1. **Use vertical 2:3 images.** This is still the easiest win. 2. **Put the keyword early in the title.** Do not bury the topic. 3. **Write a real description.** Empty descriptions are usually wasted upside. 4. **Choose the board on purpose.** Context matters more than a lot of creators assume.
That will not guarantee a viral pin. It will give the pin a fairer chance, which is usually the more useful goal.

item.title: How I Set Up PostHog in a Chrome Extension (MV3, Content Script + Background Worker)
item.description: A practical PostHog setup for Manifest V3 Chrome extensions: where to initialize it, how to handle anonymous IDs, and which events are actually worth tracking.
item.content:encoded:
Every analytics tutorial I found assumed I was building a normal web app. One runtime. One page lifecycle. One obvious place to initialize the SDK.
*A Chrome extension in V3 is not that polite.*
In Manifest V3, you have a background service worker that goes to sleep, content scripts living inside tabs, and little UI surfaces like the popup that vanish the second someone clicks away. The first time I tried to add PostHog to that setup, I realized the usual advice was not going to help much.
So this is the setup I ended up with for a Chrome extension: simple enough to maintain, anonymous by default, and good enough to answer the only questions I actually care about.
## The first decision: where PostHog should live
This is the part that matters most.
You *can* initialize PostHog in the background service worker. You get one shared place, which is nice. But the background worker cannot see the DOM, and most of the interesting product moments in my extensions happen where the user is typing or looking at something inside the page.
You *can* initialize it in the popup or options page too. That is easy, but it only works while that UI is open. For actual product usage, that felt too narrow.
I ended up initializing PostHog in the **content script**. That puts it closest to the real user action. In MV3, content scripts run in an isolated world, so PostHog's CDN setup is workable there as long as the project API key is available at build time.
I still use the background worker for extension plumbing. I just do not make it the main analytics home.
## The small build-time trick that makes this workable
The PostHog project API key is public anyway, so I stopped overthinking it and baked it into the build:
```typescript // wxt.config.ts — bake the key at build time // Set VITE_POSTHOG_PROJECT_API_KEY in your CI secrets
// telemetry.ts const POSTHOG_KEY = import.meta.env.VITE_POSTHOG_PROJECT_API_KEY; ```
That avoided adding another config fetch or permission dance. For a Chrome extension, fewer moving parts is usually the right answer.
## I use an anonymous device ID, not a user ID
I did not want email addresses, names, or anything else that would make the privacy story messy. Privacy of my users as important to me as my own privacy while using products.
So on install, I generate a random UUID and keep it in `chrome.storage.local`:
```typescript async function getOrCreateDeviceId(): Promise<string> { const stored = await chrome.storage.local.get("deviceId"); if (stored.deviceId) return stored.deviceId; const id = crypto.randomUUID(); await chrome.storage.local.set({ deviceId: id }); return id; } ```
That becomes PostHog's `distinct_id`.
It is enough to answer questions like "Did this person install and come back?" without turning the extension into a surveillance project.
## I track fewer events than I thought I would
My first instinct was to track everything. That would have been a mistake.
In practice, four events told me almost everything I needed to know:
```typescript // Install (once) posthog.capture("install", { version: chrome.runtime.getManifest().version });
// Core value action (the moment they get value) posthog.capture("subject_scored", { dimension: "title" });
// Monetization trigger posthog.capture("paywall_shown", { tier: "free", scores_used: 50 });
// Expansion action posthog.capture("rewrite_requested", { dimension: "description" }); ```
That is it.
Those four events tell me whether people are installing, reaching the value moment, hitting the limit, and asking for the "do it for me" feature. I can always add more later, but starting small kept the data readable.
## Debugging got easier once I stopped putting it in the UI
For development, I auto-enable debug mode:
```typescript const debugEnabled = import.meta.env.MODE === "development"; ```
And if I need to turn on extra logging manually, I can do it from DevTools:
```javascript chrome.storage.local.set({ debugLogging: true }); ```
I briefly considered a user-facing debug toggle. Then I imagined normal users seeing it and wondering whether something was broken. That was enough to kill the idea.
## The dashboard I actually check
This part is refreshingly unglamorous.
I set up one funnel insight: 1. Install 2. Core action 3. Paywall shown
Then I filter by `app` and look at daily trends.
That is basically the whole analytics system. I do not need 19 dashboards. I need a quick answer to: are people using the thing, and where do they stop?
## The privacy part I did not want to get wrong
A few rules I kept from day one:
- ✅ Anonymous UUID only — no PII - ✅ No page content in events, only counts and categories - ✅ Privacy policy discloses anonymous usage events - ✅ Chrome Web Store data disclosure does **not** claim personally identifiable information - ✅ Even if a UUID is often treated differently from direct personal data, I still disclose it plainly
That gave me a setup I could defend without squirming.
## If I were helping a friend do this tomorrow
I would not start with "How do I instrument everything?"
I would start with:
- one place to initialize PostHog - one anonymous identifier - four or five events that map to the funnel - one dashboard you will actually open
That gets you useful telemetry in a Chrome extension without letting analytics become its own side project.
